We interview Sandro Sbarbaro, a key figure for the historical memory of Val d’Aveto and its characters, thanks to his work as a local historian and as founder, with Mario Senoglosso, of that priceless mine of knowledge that is the website Valdaveto.net. But he is much more besides: a poet, a walker, a devotee of the mountains and of the Genoese lands. Today we talk with him about the people who have inhabited the Trebbia-Aveto ridge over the centuries.

Sandro, tell us something about banditry on the Trebbia-Aveto ridge. The Via del Cifalco must have been infested with it…

Banditry was a scourge that afflicted our Valleys for a few centuries, especially between the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. In the State Archives in Genoa lie numerous notarial files concerning the trials brought against bandits captured by the forces of law and order. They offer a glimpse of the wretched life that humble folk led in those days.

But who were these bandits?

Back then, people became bandits for a whole range of reasons, but above all because of the feuds that broke out between the various “kin groups” over “commercial” matters. Control of the territory – through the imposition of tolls and the shelter offered to the mule caravans crossing the Valleys – allowed certain “Houses” that controlled the land to devote themselves to collecting tolls, while the “pariahs” and the “disinherited” (the law of “Maggiorasco”, primogeniture, invariably favoured the firstborn son) made their way as soldiers of fortune, priests, constables, muleteers, and so on. These men, peasants included, were “ordered” by the Families to carry out punitive raids against rival clans. After committing a few crimes, they were “banished” for life; and so, once they had taken to the woods, the road to the gallows or to death by murder lay wide open.

Your website Valdaveto.net is full of stories about bandits in the area. Are there any episodes in particular that people still tell?

At Piandifontana stood the house of the bandit Luigi Brizzolara, known as Animalunga. In the nineteenth century he became a legend in Val d’Aveto (it was said that he robbed the rich to give to the poor); but his “exploits” brought him into conflict with the Law, and he was eventually killed by a carabiniere at Magnasco. In the square by the village fountain there is a cross on a stone that supposedly marks the spot where he was killed.

And what remains today?

Something always remains, for those who know how to dig. At Sbarbari, where my father’s family comes from, the old valley folk remembered well that the so-called “Ca’ de’ pégure” (House of the sheep), the first house in the village, had been founded by none other than the bandit Sbarbaro, perhaps hailing from Val di Sturla. In this dwelling, built on sloping ground and known as a “casa di pendio” (hillside house), there are still some loopholes designed for defence with the arquebus, facing what was then the public road.

In one of your writings, you argue that “[the] bandits, moreover, by feeding the flourishing market in stolen goods, with Cabanne in Val d'Aveto, Cerignale in Val Trebbia and Verzi in Val Fontanabuona as receiving areas, allowed a stifled economy to recover a little, bringing fresh capital into the area”. Nowadays the economy around here is anything but flourishing. So do we need a few new bandits?

Ah, quite so! Bandits, in various guises, have always existed. Some steal out of hunger and some do not. I side with those who steal out of hunger. History teaches us that even the bandits of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries were often oppressed for faults that probably lay further upstream. Getting by, in any case, is a resource that forgotten peoples, such as mountain peoples, sometimes devise to defend themselves somehow against the various bureaucracies.

But the Via del Cifalco, and Val Trebbia and Val d’Aveto in general, were not frequented only by bandits. There were poets and other thinkers too. Can you give us the names of the most interesting ones?

The best known was certainly Giorgio Caproni…

…But everybody knows that! We want the names of the others, the ones nobody knows.

There are quite a few poets and thinkers who have frequented Val d’Aveto, some of them our contemporaries: Rita Biggio Casazza, Vincenzo Sbarboro, Bruno Cobianchi. But…

…But?

…The one I hold in the highest regard is my friend Carlo di Francescantonio, who has ancestors in Esola, right below the Via del Cifalco. The world of poets is a phantasmagorical circus where whoever knows how to win over the public rises to the top. Carlo is an honest person, careful not to get mixed up with the snake-oil sellers.

And then you are a poet yourself.

Let’s put it that way.

All right, I won’t grill you about that. But then tell me about other characters who peopled these parts.

If I start, I’ll never stop. The first who come to mind are the Cereghino, the family of travelling storytellers known as “sciallin”, who came from Castello (between Favale di Malvaro and the Passo della Scoglina, along the Antica Via del Cifalco). They toured the fairs and markets of the Ligurian-Emilian Apennines, recounting satirical tales, news stories and folk ballads. After Andrea Cereghino bought a Bible not approved by the local clergy, in Genoa in 1849, the story goes that the whole family became Waldensian and made converts in the area, with great success! So much so that this phenomenon culminated in arrests, trials and various other persecutions for many people in the Malvaro Valley, particularly among the members of the Cereghino family.

How far do the memories of all these people speak to us of our lands as we see them today, and help us to understand them?

Telling the past is a way of meeting the future. Without memories, Man would amount to little. History is a jumble of memories. Remembering the toil of the old folk is no mere rhetoric. It is a way of reconnecting with the land they once trod and that we still tread today, simply in different footwear.

What happened in these lands at the time of the partisan Resistance? Were they truly a theatre of struggle and fervour, or do you think there is (also) a bit of rhetoric involved?

Well! Rhetoric is part of the language of lawyers, and a good part of the Resistance in the Ligurian Levante was stuffed with it. These people romanticised the events of the Resistance a bit too much, thereby creating its myth, often for party reasons. What is more, thanks to the work of some of these notables, the “sol dell’avvenir” (the “sun of the future”) ended up as a restoration of the status quo, albeit a disguised one; and that future was largely thrown away, betraying the ideas for which many had fought and died. At the end of hostilities, many partisans wondered “whether it had been worth it”.

And yet, even today, the subject is constantly evoked. In a great many villages of Val Trebbia and Val d’Aveto there are more commemorative plaques than inhabitants.

During the celebrations, people line up stiffly in front of the partisans’ memorial stones; but then the ideals of those days are often betrayed in practice. The redemption of the disinherited, which they had fought for, is now an empty word.

Would you go so far as to say that, in the past, the life of the communities in our mountains was more authentic, and the communities themselves more united?

Once upon a time, to take the case of Val d’Aveto up to the nineteenth century, there were six or seven notaries in the area, and others, such as priests, of at times questionable moral standing but deeply bound to the land. Then there was a population that, though riven by old feuds, was united in managing the “common good”: bridges, roads, land. Later, with emigration and the coming of the two world wars, each family thought more of its own particular interest than of the general one. This was also a matter of survival.

The Antica Via del Cifalco, like the other “salt roads”, establishes a link between land and sea. Can we say that, with the decline of the “salt roads”, this link has been severed in our cultural and spiritual horizons?

Undoubtedly! We must bear in mind that the “salt roads” were important not only commercially but also culturally: thanks to these mule tracks, there was a constant transfer of knowledge, both material and spiritual, from one side of the Apennines to the other. With the coming of the railways and motorways, which isolated this Apennine macro-region, the slow decline of the “lands in between” gathered pace.

What advice would you give us for making the most of the rediscovery of the Antica Via del Cifalco?

My only recommendation is to make sure the Way is walked; if not by mule caravans as in the old days, then at least by people who feel the need to reclaim the beauty that hovers all around. The charm of our Valleys sometimes does not show, because we are distracted by the thousands of artificial stimuli typical of people immersed in the digital age. Tracing a new way serves its continued use; otherwise it risks being a fine museum whose key has been lost.

As an appendix to this interview, we present two poems by Sandro Sbarbaro which, by choice, we have decided not to translate. Those who do not speak Genoese dialect will therefore have to rely entirely on the way the sounds of the words fall upon their own imagination.

A voxe do tempo

Fotografie ingiànie
sätan fêua in po' muffìe
da in'a scàtoa
scordà in sofìta

Son a voxe do tempo
ch'a te ciamma lontan
E te pa' che a tò man
a traverse in misteio

Se e lägrime poessan dì
l'amô che in chêu gonfio
o no l'à sapûo dà.

Notturno 'n campagna

'N çê scûo o fâ brillâ e stelle
comme 'n sce 'na scátoa de baxi

L'aia da nèutte
a traversa i prôuei
Chì e là rapîi
da-o canto da çigaa

M'arrembu a 'n erboo
e comme 'n can
fasso 'n po' d'ægua

L'è zà doman
